<!-- src/content/docs/explanation/design-history.mdx -->
# How v2 came to be

Version 2.0 was not an accumulation of features but a redesign driven by an
audit. This page summarizes that record — the findings, the decisions and the
non-goals — as the project itself documented it in `docs/DESIGN.md` and
`CHANGELOG.md`. Statements below are sourced from those documents; where the
*why* is unrecorded, the page presents only what the code does.

## What v1 cost

The performance audit of 1.1.0 found six structural costs. Each rendering of
a styled value allocated repeatedly: a `Vec<Attribute>` cloned on every
builder call, `String`s returned per color code, a `Vec<String>` joined into
the start sequence, and a `format!` plus text clone in `render`. Printing
re-read the environment variables on every line. And `Style` was neither
`Copy` nor `const`-constructible, so no static style tables were possible.

## What v1 lacked

The DX audit, comparing against `owo-colors`, `yansi`, `colored`, `anstyle`
and `termcolor`, found the gaps that became v2's feature list: no
multi-segment lines, no hyperlinks, no gradients, no capability detection or
degradation, no hex-string parsing, no ANSI-aware text toolkit, no
conditional styling, no macros, no panels, no contrast helper, no fallible
IO, width computed from `chars()` instead of terminal columns, and duplicate
attributes emitting duplicate codes. One finding was a naming one: `Console`
was not a console but a styled string.

## The core model decisions

The redesign landed on a small set of interlocking decisions:

- `Style` and `Effects` became `Copy`, `const`-constructible values; the
  attribute list became a `u16` bitset with canonical emission order and
  idempotent adds.
- `Span` became the primary type — text plus style plus optional OSC 8 link —
  with `Display` writing SGR codes straight into the formatter.
- `Line` became the composition primitive, with styling methods that apply to
  the last pushed span so chains read left to right.
- The deterministic-rendering philosophy of v1 was kept and made explicit:
  string rendering never consults the environment; only printing does.

## Compatibility strategy

The MSRV stayed at 1.85 (edition 2024), `unsafe` stayed forbidden, and the
crate kept zero runtime dependencies. `Console` remains a type alias of
`Span`, so most 1.x code keeps compiling. Three breaking changes were accepted
and documented: canonical, deduplicated attribute codes; `Style::attributes()`
returning the `Effects` bitset instead of `&[Attribute]`; and the `insta`
snapshot dev-dependency replaced by exact-string contract tests. The
[migration guide](/guides/migrate-from-v1/) turns these into steps.

## Non-goals

The design document names what v2 deliberately does not do:

- Window-size queries, cursor control and alternate screens — the territory
  of terminal-control crates.
- Full Unicode width parity with the `unicode-width` crate — the built-in
  table covers the common CJK, emoji and combining ranges, documented as an
  approximation in service of the zero-dependency guarantee.

These boundaries are stable design positions, not missing features; a PR
introducing either would be reversing a recorded decision rather than filling
a gap.

## Next steps

<!-- src/content/docs/explanation/rendering-model.mdx -->
# Deterministic rendering

pretty-console draws a sharp line between two ways output leaves your
program. Understanding it predicts what your tests, logs and terminals will
show. This page is an observation of documented and tested behavior in
`src/lib.rs`, `src/span.rs` and `src/style.rs`.

## Two paths, two contracts

| Path | Members | Environment |
| --- | --- | --- |
| String rendering | `render`, `render_with`, `to_string`, `Display` | Never consulted |
| Printing | `print`, `println`, `eprint`, `eprintln`, `try_*`, `write_to` | Honors `ColorChoice` |

The same [`Span`](/reference/span/) renders identically on a CI runner and in
an interactive terminal. Printing, on the other hand, decides at call time
whether to write the rendered string or the plain text, based on the global
[`ColorChoice`](/reference/color-control/).

## What determinism buys you

- Exact-output tests (`assert_eq!` on `to_string()`) are stable across
  machines, shells and CI — the project itself relies on this in its contract
  tests.
- Logs written to files keep their escapes (or keep none, if you render
  explicitly) regardless of where the program ran.
- `format!` never changes its mind between environments.

The cost is that `to_string()` alone cannot respect `NO_COLOR` — that is a
printing concern by design, and the boundary is deliberate.

## The print family's environment contract

When a print method runs, it checks whether colors are enabled. If yes, the
rendered string goes to the stream; if no, the plain text does — the same
bytes a `strip_ansi` of the rendered string would produce, with no leftover
escape codes and no link sequences. This is why
[`Span::link`](/reference/span/) needs no special handling in plain mode:
the plain branch never emits it.

## Canonical ordering and idempotence

Within one ANSI sequence, attributes are emitted first — in the fixed order
bold, dim, italic, underline, blink, reverse, hidden, strikethrough — then
the foreground color, then the background color. Two properties follow:

1. The same style always produces the same byte sequence, whatever order the
   builder methods were called in.
2. Repeating an attribute changes nothing; the bitset cannot hold a duplicate.

Both properties are covered by exact-string contract tests in the repository
(`tests/contract.rs`), and both are v2 changes — v1 emitted attributes in
insertion order with possible duplicates.

## Plain styles emit nothing

A style with no colors and no attributes is *plain*, and a plain span renders
as its bare text: no start sequence, no reset. The reset is only written when
a start sequence was. So `Span::new("hi").to_string()` is exactly `"hi"` —
relevant when you conditionally style and do not want empty `ESC [m` noise.

## The no-color feature

The compile-time `no-color` feature removes ANSI generation from the binary
entirely. Every method still exists and behaves as a pass-through:
`is_color_enabled()` returns `false`, links are suppressed, and the text
tools, `Panel` and level helpers keep working. The distinction from
`ColorChoice::Never` is binary size and the impossibility of re-enabling at
runtime.

## Next steps

<!-- src/content/docs/explanation/zero-cost-design.mdx -->
# The zero-cost design

pretty-console describes itself as *zero-cost*. This page explains what that
means concretely — where the costs went, and what remains. The decisions
recorded here come from the project's own design document
(`docs/DESIGN.md` in the repository) and from the code itself.

## What zero-cost means here

The crate never allocates while *rendering* a styled value into a formatter,
and it never re-reads the environment while printing. Allocation still
happens where it is inherent: `Span` owns a `String`, and a `Line` owns its
`Vec<Span>`. What is gone is the hidden tax most styling libraries pay per
rendered value.

## Styles are values, not builders with state

`Style` is a small `Copy` struct — an optional foreground, an optional
background, an attribute bitset. Building, merging and cloning a style
compiles to register moves. A v1-style `Vec<Attribute>` was the audit's
first finding: every builder call cloned a heap list. In v2 the whole style
can live in a `const`:

```rust
use pretty_console::{Color, Style};

const HEADING: Style = Style::new().bold().underline().fg(Color::BRIGHT_BLUE);
```

## The Effects bitset

Attributes live in a `u16` bitset, one bit per attribute. Consequences that
matter beyond memory:

- `.bold().bold()` emits one code, not two — duplicates are structurally
  impossible.
- Emission order is fixed by bit order (bold → strikethrough), not by call
  order, which makes output contract-testable.
- `merge` is a single `or`.

## Writing codes straight into the formatter

`Display` for `Span` writes the SGR start sequence, the text, and the reset
directly into the destination `fmt::Formatter`. There is no intermediate
`String` in `write!`/`print!` paths, and the decimal digits of SGR parameters
are written without going through `format!`. The audit counted at least five
allocations per render in v1; the v2 render path has none.

## One environment decision, cached

Deciding whether colors are enabled inspects several environment variables
and stdout. Doing that per printed line costs syscalls. v2 performs the
`Auto` decision once and caches it in an atomic; `set_color_choice`
invalidates the cache. After the first print, the hot path performs no
environment access at all.

## Visible width in a single pass

`truncate` and `pad` measure and rewrite in one pass over the input, with a
byte scanner for `strip_ansi` that searches for the next `ESC` and copies
slices between them. The width table itself covers the common CJK, emoji and
combining ranges without pulling in the `unicode-width` crate — a documented
trade-off between exactness and the zero-dependency guarantee.

## What this does not cover

The benchmark numbers in the repository README were measured on a CI-class
Linux VM; reproduce them with `cargo run --release --example bench` before
treating them as your own numbers. And "zero-cost" is about allocation and
syscalls — terminal rendering itself, and the width approximation above,
remain practical approximations of what any terminal does.

## Next steps

<!-- src/content/docs/guides/decorations.mdx -->
# Add gradients, panels and hyperlinks

This guide shows how to produce the decorative output forms: per-character
gradients, rainbows, rounded panels with inlaid titles, and clickable
hyperlinks. It assumes you can print a styled [`Span`](/reference/span/).

## Fade a gradient across text

`gradient` interpolates from one color to another, one character at a time,
and returns a [`Line`](/reference/line/):

```rust
use pretty_console::{gradient, Color};

gradient("sunrise fade", Color::hex(0xFF3E6C), Color::hex(0x4DC4FF)).println();
```

`gradient_bg` does the same for backgrounds. Both honor
[`ColorChoice`](/reference/color-control/) when printing, and both can be
pre-degraded with `render_with` like any line.

## Paint a rainbow

`rainbow` cycles the full hue wheel across the text's characters:

```rust
use pretty_console::rainbow;

rainbow("the full spectrum, one hue per character").println();
```

`rainbow_bg` paints the same spectrum as backgrounds. Whitespace is colored
too — the spectrum covers every character, not every visible glyph — and each
character is its own span, so the resulting line's `spans()` has one entry per
character.

## Build a titled panel

`Panel` draws a rounded box with an optional title inlaid into the top border.
Content lines accept a [`Line`](/reference/line/), a
[`Span`](/reference/span/), or a plain string:

```rust
use pretty_console::{Line, Panel, Span, Style, Styled};

Panel::new()
    .title("Summary")
    .border(Style::new().bright_black())
    .line(Line::new().push("passed: ").dim().push("128").green().bold())
    .line("skipped: 3".dim())
    .line(Span::new("failed: 0").green())
    .println();
```

The inner width fits the widest line plus padding by default; the title can
widen the box. Only the border characters and the title divider take the
border style — content keeps its own colors.

## Fix the panel width

`width` sets the inner content width explicitly. It acts as a floor for the
title and truncates over-wide lines with an ellipsis:

```rust
use pretty_console::Panel;

let panel = Panel::new()
    .title("Build report")
    .width(40)
    .line("a very long status line that will be cut");
panel.println();
```

When a line exceeds the fixed width, `render` cuts it at the visible-width
budget and appends `…`, so the box never breaks its own border. Drop the
`.width(40)` call to let the box size itself.

## Make text clickable with OSC 8

`link` attaches a hyperlink. Supporting terminals make the text clickable;
others ignore the sequence:

```rust
use pretty_console::{Span, Styled};

Span::new("pretty-console on GitHub")
    .blue()
    .underline()
    .link("https://github.com/elcoosp/pretty-console")
    .println();
```

The link wraps the styled text and is removed by `unlink()`; `url()` returns
it for inspection. Links are emitted only when printing with colors enabled —
with colors off, or under the `no-color` feature, the plain text prints.

# Degrade colors

This guide shows how to detect what a terminal can display and how to render
truecolor content at a lower capability level. Use it when output must survive
CI logs, `ssh` sessions or IDE consoles that only understand a subset of ANSI
colors. For turning colors off entirely, see
[Control colors at runtime](/guides/runtime-color-control/).

## Detect the terminal capability

`supports_color_level()` inspects `FORCE_COLOR`, `CLICOLOR_FORCE`, `NO_COLOR`,
`CLICOLOR`, `TERM` and `COLORTERM`, then falls back to stdout detection. It
returns `None` when no colors should be emitted at all:

```rust
use pretty_console::{supports_color_level, ColorLevel};

match supports_color_level() {
    Some(ColorLevel::TrueColor) => println!("terminal can display everything"),
    Some(level) => println!("terminal degrades to {level:?}"),
    None => println!("no colors at all"),
}
```

## Render a span or line at a level

`render_with` reduces every color of the styled value to the richest
representation the level supports. Unlike `render`, it exists for exactly this
situation — pre-degrading before you ship the string somewhere else:

```rust
use pretty_console::{ColorLevel, Line, Span, Styled};

let fancy = "truecolor text".fg_hex(0x7C_4D_FF);
println!("{}", fancy.render_with(ColorLevel::Ansi256)); // nearest palette entry
println!("{}", fancy.render_with(ColorLevel::Ansi16));  // nearest of the 16 base colors

let line = Line::new().push("done ").push("fast").fg_hex(0x22_D3_EE);
println!("{}", line.render_with(ColorLevel::Ansi16));
```

The returned string is plain text with the degraded escapes baked in — write it
to logs, a pipe or a file as-is.

## Degrade a single color

`Color` exposes the same reduction so you can render palette swatches or
legends that match the degraded output:

```rust
use pretty_console::{Color, ColorLevel};

let brand = Color::hex(0x7C_4D_FF);
let for_256 = brand.degrade_to(ColorLevel::Ansi256);
let for_16 = brand.degrade_to(ColorLevel::Ansi16);
```

`degrade_to` keeps colors that the level can represent exactly (a base color
stays itself at `Ansi16`), maps RGB to the nearest 256-palette entry, and maps
anything to the nearest of the 16 base colors at `Ansi16`.

## Produce stable output for CI logs

Combine detection and degradation in one place, early in `main`:

```rust
use pretty_console::{supports_color_level, ColorLevel, Span, Styled};

fn render_report(body: &str) -> String {
    let level = supports_color_level().unwrap_or(ColorLevel::Ansi16);
    Span::new(body).bold().render_with(level)
}
```

On a color-less runner, `supports_color_level()` returns `None` and the
`unwrap_or` keeps your pipeline rendering (as plain 16-color output); pick
`ColorChoice::Never` instead if you want no escapes at all — see
[Control colors at runtime](/guides/runtime-color-control/).

## Next steps

<!-- src/content/docs/guides/exact-colors.mdx -->
# Use exact colors

This guide shows how to apply exact colors from a design system, how to parse
color strings from configuration or CLI flags, and how to choose a readable
foreground for an arbitrary background. It assumes you can print a styled
[`Span`](/reference/span/).

## Use a packed hex value

`Color::hex` builds a 24-bit RGB color from a `0xRRGGBB` value, and
`fg_hex` / `bg_hex` apply it inline:

```rust
use pretty_console::{Color, Span, Styled};

Span::new("Violet").fg(Color::hex(0x7C_4D_FF)).println();
Span::new("Violet").fg_hex(0x7C_4D_FF).println();
Span::new("Highlight").bg_hex(0x1E_29_3B).println();
```

`Color::hex(0x00FF7F)` equals `Color::RGB(0, 255, 127)` — the packed value is
split into three bytes, highest first.

## Parse a hex string from config or CLI

`Color::from_hex_str` accepts `"#7c4dff"`, `"7c4dff"` and the three-digit
shorthand `"#f0a"`. It returns a `ParseColorError` instead of panicking, so it
fits configuration pipelines:

```rust
use pretty_console::{Color, Span};

let theme_color = "#22d3ee";
match Color::from_hex_str(theme_color) {
    Ok(color) => Span::new("theme accent").fg(color).println(),
    Err(err) => eprintln!("bad color {theme_color:?}: {err}"),
}
```

`Color` also implements `FromStr`, so `"#22d3ee".parse::<Color>()` works with
libraries that parse from strings generically. Errors come in two variants:
`InvalidLength` (the string is not 3 or 6 hex digits, ignoring an optional
leading `#`) and `InvalidDigit(char)` (a character is not a hex digit).

## Use 256-palette entries

For terminals where palette identity matters, `Color::indexed(n)` selects an
entry of the 256-color table, and the sixteen constants
`Color::BLACK`…`Color::BRIGHT_WHITE` cover the base palette:

```rust
use pretty_console::{Color, Span, Styled};

Span::new("sky").fg(Color::indexed(117)).println();
Span::new("base red").fg(Color::RED).println();
```

Palette entries render as `38;5;n` (foreground) and `48;5;n` (background);
RGB colors render as `38;2;r;g;b` and `48;2;r;g;b`. See
[`Color`](/reference/color/) for the exact codes.

## Pick a readable foreground for a background

`readable_on` returns black or white — whichever meets the WCAG 4.5:1
contrast threshold against the color you call it on:

```rust
use pretty_console::{Color, Span, Styled};

let bg = Color::hex(0x1E_29_3B);
Span::new("readable").bg(bg).fg(bg.readable_on()).println();
```

Use it whenever a user-configurable background could be any color; the badge
stays readable on near-black and near-white alike. `luminance()` exposes the
underlying WCAG relative luminance if you need custom thresholds.

## Next steps

<!-- src/content/docs/guides/migrate-from-v1.mdx -->
# Migrate from 1.x

This guide lists the concrete steps for upgrading from pretty-console 1.x to
2.0, with the exact breaking changes and their fixes. For the reasoning behind
the redesign, see [How v2 came to be](/explanation/design-history/).

## Bump the dependency

```sh
cargo add pretty-console@2.0.0
```

2.0 needs Rust 1.85 or newer (edition 2024). Check your `rust-toolchain.toml`
and CI matrix before continuing.

## Keep or rename Console

`Console` still exists as a type alias of [`Span`](/reference/span/), so
existing `Console::new("...").red().println()` code keeps compiling. New code
should spell the type `Span`:

```rust
use pretty_console::Span;

// Before: Console::new("hi").red();
// Now:
let span = Span::new("hi").red();
```

`Console::new_with_style` also keeps working; the Span-native spellings are
`Span::new_with_style(text, style)` and `Style::paint(text)`.

## Fix exact-output tests

Attribute codes are now emitted in **canonical order** (bold → dim → italic →
underline → blink → reverse → hidden → strikethrough), followed by the
foreground color, then the background color — not insertion order — and
duplicates are removed. If you snapshot exact escape strings, update them:

```rust
// Before (1.x, insertion order, duplicates possible):
//   bold().bold() could emit "1;1"
// Now: one code, canonical position:
assert_eq!(
    Span::new("hi").bold().bold().to_string(),
    "\x1b[1mhi\x1b[0m"
);
```

The `insta` snapshot dev-dependency is gone; the project itself now asserts
exact strings in contract tests. If you depended on `insta` only for
pretty-console output, plain `assert_eq!` on `to_string()` is the supported
replacement.

## Update attributes() consumers

`Style::attributes()` used to hand out `&[Attribute]`. It now returns an
`Effects` bitset — a `Copy` value with `has`, `contains`, `insert`, `remove`,
`union` and an `attributes()` iterator:

```rust
use pretty_console::{Attribute, Style, Styled};

let style = Style::new().bold().underline();
let effects = style.attributes();
assert!(effects.has(Attribute::Bold));
assert_eq!(effects.attributes().count(), 2);
```

Code that matched on slice contents should query the bitset with
`has(Attribute::…)` or `contains(Effects::…)` instead.

## Adopt the Span-native spellings

The following renames are mechanical:

| 1.x | 2.0 |
| --- | --- |
| `Console` | `Span` (alias kept) |
| `Console::new_with_style` | `Span::new_with_style` / `Style::paint` |
| `&[Attribute]` from `attributes()` | `Effects` bitset |
| insertion-order attribute codes | canonical order, deduplicated |

Everything else — level helpers, `banner`, the `Styled` trait — kept its v1
signature.

## Next steps

<!-- src/content/docs/guides/reusable-styles.mdx -->
# Reuse and merge styles

This guide shows how to define a reusable `Style`, apply it to different
texts, and combine styles without duplicating attributes. It assumes you
already install the crate and print spans — see
[Getting started](/tutorials/getting-started/) if you do not.

## Define a style once

`Style` is `Copy` and `const`-constructible, so a style can live in a `const`
or `static` and never allocate:

```rust
use pretty_console::{Color, Style};

const HEADING: Style = Style::new().bold().underline().fg(Color::BRIGHT_BLUE);

HEADING.paint("Chapter 1").println();
HEADING.paint("Chapter 2").println();
```

`Style::paint(text)` produces a ready-to-print [`Span`](/reference/span/).

## Apply it to different text

When you already hold a styled [`Span`](/reference/span/) and want to keep its
style but change the text, use `with_text`:

```rust
use pretty_console::{Span, Styled};

let error = Span::new("").red().bold();
error.with_text("Error 1: Something went wrong").println();
error.with_text("Error 2: Another issue").println();
```

## Merge two styles

`merge` combines two styles: colors set by the argument win, and attribute
sets are unioned — duplicates are impossible because attributes live in a
bitset:

```rust
use pretty_console::{Color, Style};

let heading = Style::new().bold().underline().fg(Color::BRIGHT_BLUE);
let emphasis = Style::new().fg(Color::RED);

// Red wins; bold and underline stay.
heading.merge(emphasis).paint("Important").println();
```

This is the rule to remember when layering a base style with an override:
the override's foreground and background replace the base's, attributes from
both sides are kept.

## Convert colors and attributes into styles

`Style` implements `From<Color>`, `From<Attribute>` and `From<Effects>`, so
single-purpose values convert directly:

```rust
use pretty_console::{Attribute, Color, Style};

let colored = Style::from(Color::CYAN);
let tilted = Style::from(Attribute::Italic);
```

## Adjust conditionally with `when`

`when` keeps builder chains flat instead of forcing `if` statements around
them:

```rust
use pretty_console::{Color, Style};

let verbose = std::env::var("VERBOSE").is_ok();
let style = Style::new().when(verbose, |s| s.fg(Color::CYAN).dim());
```

The closure runs only when the condition holds; otherwise the style passes
through untouched. [`Span`](/reference/span/) and
[`Line`](/reference/line/) have the same `when` method.

## Next steps

<!-- src/content/docs/guides/runtime-color-control.mdx -->
# Control colors at runtime

This guide shows how printed output decides between styled and plain text, how
to wire that decision into your own `--color` flag, and how to print without
panicking on closed pipes. For lowering the color *depth* instead of switching
colors off, see [Degrade colors](/guides/degrade-colors/).

## Default behavior

The print family — `print`, `println`, `eprint`, `eprintln` and `write_to` —
honors a global [`ColorChoice`](/reference/color-control/). The default,
`Auto`, checks the environment and stdout:

```rust
use pretty_console::{Span, Styled};

// Styled when colors are enabled, plain text otherwise.
Span::new("hello").red().println();
```

The detection runs once, is cached, and never touches the environment again on
the hot printing path. String rendering (`to_string`, `render`, `Display`) is
unaffected — see [Deterministic rendering](/explanation/rendering-model/) for
why.

## The environment variables pretty-console honors

| Variable | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `FORCE_COLOR` | `0` turns colors off; `1`/`2`/`3` force them on (Node.js convention); empty means unset |
| `CLICOLOR_FORCE` | Any non-`0` value forces colors on |
| `NO_COLOR` | Any non-empty value disables colors ([no-color.org](https://no-color.org/)) |
| `CLICOLOR` | `0` disables colors |
| `TERM` | `dumb` disables colors |
| `COLORTERM` | `truecolor`/`24bit` advertises truecolor capability (used by detection, not by the on/off switch) |

`FORCE_COLOR` wins over `CLICOLOR_FORCE`; forcing variables win over
disabling ones. The exact precedence lives in
[`Color control`](/reference/color-control/).

## Wire a --color flag

Set the global choice after parsing your CLI arguments. `Auto` restores
environment-driven behavior:

```rust
use pretty_console::{set_color_choice, ColorChoice, Span, Styled};

enum ColorFlag {
    Always,
    Never,
    Auto,
}

fn main() {
    let flag = parse_color_flag(); // your --color handling
    set_color_choice(match flag {
        ColorFlag::Always => ColorChoice::Always,
        ColorFlag::Never => ColorChoice::Never,
        ColorFlag::Auto => ColorChoice::Auto,
    });

    Span::new("styled or plain, decided above").cyan().println();
}
```

`set_color_choice` invalidates the cached `Auto` decision, so the next print
re-evaluates if you switch back to `Auto`.

## Print to stderr

Diagnostics belong on stderr; the `e*` variants behave like their stdout
siblings and honor the same choice:

```rust
use pretty_console::{Span, Styled};

Span::error("Disk full").eprintln();
```

## Handle broken pipes with try_*

The plain print methods panic when the underlying stream fails — for example
when stdout is a closed pipe (`myapp | head -n 1`). The `try_*` variants
return `io::Result<()>` instead:

```rust
use pretty_console::{Span, Styled};

if Span::new("streaming…").dim().try_println().is_err() {
    // downstream closed the pipe — exit quietly
}
```

`write_to` does the same for any writer you hold:

```rust
use pretty_console::{Span, Styled};

fn main() -> std::io::Result<()> {
    let mut buffer: Vec<u8> = Vec::new();
    Span::new("logged").green().write_to(&mut buffer)?;
    Ok(())
}
```

## Next steps

<!-- src/content/docs/guides/status-lines.mdx -->
# Compose status lines

This guide shows how to build a single row out of differently styled segments,
how the styling methods attach to segments, and how to align whole lines. It
assumes you can already print a styled [`Span`](/reference/span/).

## Push segments left to right

[`Line`](/reference/line/) collects spans and renders them as one row. Push a
segment, then style it — the styling methods always apply to the **last
pushed** segment:

```rust
use pretty_console::Line;

let line = Line::new()
    .push("  build ").dim()
    .push("cargo build --release").bold()
    .push(" finished in ").push("4.2s").green();
line.println();
```

Read the chain as a cursor: `.push("...")` moves the cursor to a new segment;
`.dim()`, `.bold()` and `.green()` restyle the segment under the cursor. The
connector `" finished in "` gets no styling calls, so it stays plain.

## Understand the last-span rule

Because styling applies to the last pushed segment, the order of `push` and
style calls decides what gets colored:

```rust
use pretty_console::Line;

// Red applies to "world", not to "hello ".
let line = Line::new().push("hello ").push("world").red();
```

If you style before pushing anything, the line creates an empty trailing
segment and styles that — harmless, but pointless. Style after the `push`
whose segment you mean to color.

## Build a line from an iterator

For segments that already exist as spans, construct directly:

```rust
use pretty_console::{Line, Span, Styled};

let spans = vec![
    "status: ".styled(),
    Span::new("ok").green().bold(),
];
let line = Line::from_spans(spans);
```

`Line` also implements `FromIterator<Span>` and `From<Vec<Span>>`, so
`collect()` works on span iterators.

## Restyle every span at once

`with_style` merges a style into **every** span of the line; the merged
style's colors win over per-span colors, attributes are unioned:

```rust
use pretty_console::{Line, Style};

let line = Line::new().push("a ").push("b").red();
let dimmed = line.with_style(Style::new().dim());
```

`map_span` rewrites each span through a closure when you need per-span logic.

## Accumulate in a loop

In loops, collect the row by reassigning the builder — [`Line`](/reference/line/)
methods consume and return the line (`push_mut` appends in place when you do
not need to style the new segment):

```rust
use pretty_console::Line;

let mut line = Line::new();
for (name, ok) in [("fmt", true), ("clippy", true), ("tests", false)] {
    line = line.push(name);
    if ok {
        line = line.push(" ✓").green();
    } else {
        line = line.push(" ✗").red();
    }
    line = line.push("  ");
}
line.println();
```

## Align a whole line with format widths

`Display` for `Line` pads by the line's **visible** width — ANSI escapes and
wide CJK characters are measured the way a terminal renders them:

```rust
use pretty_console::Line;

let line = Line::new().push("cache ").push("warm").green();
println!("{:<20}|", line);
```

Left, right and center alignment follow the standard format spec, and the
padding is computed from visible columns — so columns line up even when the
segments contain escapes or CJK text.

## Next steps

<!-- src/content/docs/guides/text-layout.mdx -->
# Measure, truncate and pad text

This guide shows how to measure, truncate and pad strings exactly the way a
terminal renders them — including strings that already contain ANSI escapes or
wide characters. Use it whenever you lay out tables, progress bars or columns.
For the full escape grammar and range tables, see
[Text tools](/reference/text-tools/).

## Measure visible width correctly

`visible_width` counts terminal columns. Escape sequences count as zero, wide
CJK characters count as two, combining marks count as zero:

```rust
use pretty_console::{visible_width, Styled};

assert_eq!(visible_width("héllo"), 5);
assert_eq!(visible_width("日本語"), 6);          // three wide chars
assert_eq!(visible_width(&"hi".red().to_string()), 2); // escapes are zero-width
```

The single-character building block is `char_width`.

## Truncate to a column budget

`truncate` cuts at `max_width` visible columns and appends the tail when
truncation happens:

```rust
use pretty_console::truncate;

assert_eq!(truncate("hello world", 8, "…"), "hello w…");
assert_eq!(truncate("short", 8, "…"), "short");
```

Three details matter in real pipelines:

1. Escape sequences survive and do not count toward the budget — styled
   strings truncate to the same visible shape as plain ones.
2. If any escape was emitted, a reset sequence is appended after the tail, so
   truncation cannot leak styles into the rest of your output.
3. When `max_width` is smaller than the tail, the tail overruns the budget
   rather than disappearing — check your minimum widths.

## Pad and align columns

`pad` widens a string to exactly `width` visible columns with a fill
character, choosing a side through `Align`:

```rust
use pretty_console::{pad, Align};

assert_eq!(pad("hi", 4, Align::Left, '.'), "hi..");
assert_eq!(pad("hi", 4, Align::Right, '.'), "..hi");
assert_eq!(pad("hi", 5, Align::Center, '.'), ".hi..");
```

`pad` never cuts: an input wider than `width` comes back unchanged. Combine
with `truncate` when you need both directions.

## Rely on format-width padding for styled values

`Display` for [`Span`](/reference/span/) and [`Line`](/reference/line/)
computes padding from visible width, so standard format specs align styled
values without extra work:

```rust
use pretty_console::Styled;

let rows = [("fmt", "ok"), ("clippy", "ok"), ("tests", "failed")];
for (name, status) in rows {
    let status_span = if status == "ok" {
        status.green()
    } else {
        status.red().bold()
    };
    println!("{:<10}| {}", name, status_span);
}
```

The `{:<10}` pads the plain name; the styled status needs no padding
compensation, because `{}` on a span never counts its escapes. This is the
difference from `format!("{:<10}", "hi".red().to_string())`, which would pad
the escaped string to the wrong visual width — use `pad` for pre-rendered
strings.

## Next steps

<!-- src/content/docs/reference/color-control.mdx -->
# Color control

The choice module controls whether printed output carries colors and what the
terminal can display. Sources: `src/choice.rs`.

## ColorChoice

`pub enum ColorChoice { Auto, Always, Never }` — derives `Debug`, `Clone`,
`Copy`, `Default`, `PartialEq`, `Eq`, `Hash`; the default is `Auto`.

| Variant | Behavior when printing |
| --- | --- |
| `Auto` (default) | Inspect the environment, then stdout tty detection — decision cached |
| `Always` | Always emit colors |
| `Never` | Never emit colors |

Only the print family honors the choice (`print`, `println`, `eprint`,
`eprintln`, `try_*`, `write_to`). String rendering never does — see
[Deterministic rendering](/explanation/rendering-model/).

## Setting and reading the choice

| Function | Signature | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `set_color_choice` | `pub fn set_color_choice(choice: ColorChoice)` | Stores the choice and invalidates the `Auto` cache |
| `color_choice` | `pub fn color_choice() -> ColorChoice` | The current global choice |

## is_color_enabled

`pub fn is_color_enabled() -> bool` — whether colors should be emitted now.

- With the `no-color` feature: always `false`.
- `Always` → `true`; `Never` → `false`.
- `Auto` → the environment decision, computed once and cached in an atomic
  (`0` unknown, `1` false, `2` true); `set_color_choice` resets the cache.
  The environment check treats empty or whitespace-only values as unset.

The `Auto` checks, in order:

1. `FORCE_COLOR` set to a non-empty value other than `0` forces colors on; `FORCE_COLOR=0` forces them off.
2. `CLICOLOR_FORCE` set to a non-empty value other than `0` forces colors on.
3. `NO_COLOR` set to a non-empty value disables colors.
4. `CLICOLOR=0` disables colors.
5. `TERM=dumb` disables colors.
6. Otherwise colors are emitted only when stdout is a terminal.

## supports_color_level

`pub fn supports_color_level() -> Option<ColorLevel>` — the richest color mode
the terminal can display exactly, or `None` when no colors should be emitted
at all. Detection order:

1. `FORCE_COLOR`: `0` → `None`, `1` → `Ansi16`, `2` → `Ansi256`, anything else → `TrueColor`
2. `CLICOLOR_FORCE` (non-zero) → `Ansi16`
3. `NO_COLOR` → `None`
4. `CLICOLOR=0` → `None`
5. `TERM=dumb` → `None`
6. `COLORTERM` of `truecolor` or `24bit` → `TrueColor`
7. `TERM` containing `256color` → `Ansi256`; `TERM` containing `direct` → `TrueColor`; any other `TERM` → `Ansi16`
8. A tty stdout → `TrueColor`
9. Otherwise `None`

## ColorLevel

`pub enum ColorLevel { Ansi16, Ansi256, TrueColor }` — derives `Debug`,
`Clone`, `Copy`, `Default`, `PartialEq`, `Eq`, `PartialOrd`, `Ord`, `Hash`;
the default is `Ansi16`. The `Ord` ordering runs from least to most capable.

## Environment variables

| Variable | Effect on enabling | Effect on capability |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `FORCE_COLOR` | `0` off; non-`0` on | `1` → Ansi16, `2` → Ansi256, `3`/other → TrueColor |
| `CLICOLOR_FORCE` | non-`0` forces on | forces Ansi16 |
| `NO_COLOR` | non-empty disables | disables |
| `CLICOLOR` | `0` disables | disables |
| `TERM` | `dumb` disables | `256color` → Ansi256, `direct` → TrueColor, other → Ansi16 |
| `COLORTERM` | — | `truecolor`/`24bit` → TrueColor |

`FORCE_COLOR` wins over `CLICOLOR_FORCE`; both win over `NO_COLOR`. Empty
values count as unset everywhere.

## Next steps

import { LinkCard } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

<LinkCard title="Control colors at runtime" description="The task-oriented guide, including --color flag wiring." href="/guides/runtime-color-control/" />

<!-- src/content/docs/reference/color.mdx -->
# Color

`Color` is a `Copy` enum: `Color::Named(u8)` is a palette index into the
256-color table, `Color::RGB(u8, u8, u8)` is a 24-bit color. It derives
`Debug`, `Clone`, `Copy`, `PartialEq`, `Eq`, `Hash`. Source: `src/color.rs`.

## Constants and constructors

The sixteen base palette entries, in index order:

| Constant | Index | Constant | Index |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `BLACK` | 0 | `BRIGHT_BLACK` | 8 |
| `RED` | 1 | `BRIGHT_RED` | 9 |
| `GREEN` | 2 | `BRIGHT_GREEN` | 10 |
| `YELLOW` | 3 | `BRIGHT_YELLOW` | 11 |
| `BLUE` | 4 | `BRIGHT_BLUE` | 12 |
| `MAGENTA` | 5 | `BRIGHT_MAGENTA` | 13 |
| `CYAN` | 6 | `BRIGHT_CYAN` | 14 |
| `WHITE` | 7 | `BRIGHT_WHITE` | 15 |

| Constructor | Signature | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `indexed` | `pub const fn indexed(index: u8) -> Self` | Same as `Color::Named(index)` |
| `rgb` | `pub const fn rgb(red: u8, green: u8, blue: u8) -> Self` | 24-bit color |
| `hex` | `pub const fn hex(value: u32) -> Self` | Packed `0xRRGGBB`; `hex(0x00FF7F)` is `RGB(0, 255, 127)` |

## Parsing hex strings

| Member | Signature | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `from_hex_str` | `pub fn from_hex_str(input: &str) -> Result<Self, ParseColorError>` | Accepts `"#7c4dff"`, `"7c4dff"`, `"#f0a"` |
| `FromStr` | `type Err = ParseColorError` | Delegates to `from_hex_str` |

`ParseColorError` derives `Debug`, `Clone`, `Copy`, `PartialEq`, `Eq`, `Hash`
and implements `Error` + `Display`:

| Variant | Display message |
| --- | --- |
| `InvalidLength` | `invalid color: expected 3 or 6 hex digits, optionally prefixed with '#'` |
| `InvalidDigit(char)` | `invalid hex digit: '…'` |

## SGR parameter accessors

| Member | Signature | Output |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `fg_code` | `pub fn fg_code(&self) -> String` | `38;5;n` (palette) or `38;2;r;g;b` (RGB) |
| `bg_code` | `pub fn bg_code(&self) -> String` | `48;5;n` or `48;2;r;g;b` |

These allocate for convenience; the render machinery writes the same
parameters into the formatter without an intermediate `String`.

## Color math

| Member | Signature | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `rgb_value` | `pub fn rgb_value(&self) -> (u8, u8, u8)` | Concrete sRGB triple; palette entries resolved through the standard xterm palette |
| `luminance` | `pub fn luminance(&self) -> f32` | WCAG sRGB relative luminance, `0.0` (black) to `1.0` (white) |
| `readable_on` | `pub fn readable_on(&self) -> Color` | White when `luminance() <= 0.17832548`, else black — the WCAG 4.5:1 crossover |
| `lerp` | `pub fn lerp(self, other: Self, t: f32) -> Self` | Linear interpolation in RGB space; `t` clamped, `t <= 0` yields `self`, `t >= 1` yields `other` |

## Degradation

| Member | Signature | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `to_256` | `pub fn to_256(self) -> Self` | Nearest 256-palette entry: the 6×6×6 cube (levels `0, 95, 135, 175, 215, 255`) versus the 24-step grayscale ramp (232–255), whichever is closer |
| `to_16` | `pub fn to_16(self) -> Self` | Nearest of the sixteen base colors, by squared RGB distance |
| `degrade_to` | `pub fn degrade_to(self, level: ColorLevel) -> Self` | `TrueColor` → unchanged; `Ansi256` → RGB to `to_256`, palette unchanged; `Ansi16` → palette indices ≤ 15 unchanged, everything else to `to_16` |
| `level` | `pub fn level(self) -> ColorLevel` | Minimum level for exact display: palette ≤ 15 → `Ansi16`, palette > 15 → `Ansi256`, RGB → `TrueColor` |

## palette_rgb

`pub fn palette_rgb(index: u8) -> (u8, u8, u8)` resolves any 256-palette
index to its standard xterm RGB value: indices 0–15 use the base table,
16–231 the 6×6×6 cube, 232–255 the grayscale ramp `8 + 10·(index − 232)`.

## Trait impls

| Impl | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `From<u8>` | `Color::Named(index)` |
| `From<(u8, u8, u8)>` | `Color::RGB(r, g, b)` |
| `FromStr` | Hex string parsing, same as `from_hex_str` |

## Next steps

import { LinkCard } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

<LinkCard title="Degrade colors" description="The task-oriented guide to capability levels." href="/guides/degrade-colors/" />

<!-- src/content/docs/reference/decorations.mdx -->
# Gradient and rainbow functions

The decoration functions paint one [`Line`](/reference/line/) whose spans are
the text's characters, each carrying its own interpolated color. All are
`#[must_use]` and none allocate beyond the resulting line. Source:
`src/decorate.rs`.

## Function signatures

| Function | Signature | Paints |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `gradient` | `pub fn gradient(text: &str, from: Color, to: Color) -> Line` | Foreground interpolation `from` → `to` |
| `gradient_bg` | `pub fn gradient_bg(text: &str, from: Color, to: Color) -> Line` | Background interpolation |
| `rainbow` | `pub fn rainbow(text: &str) -> Line` | Foreground cycling the full hue wheel |
| `rainbow_bg` | `pub fn rainbow_bg(text: &str) -> Line` | Background cycling the full hue wheel |

## Interpolation details

- Every character is its own span; `line.spans()` has one entry per
  character, whitespace included.
- The interpolation parameter is `t = i / (count − 1)` for character `i`; a
  single-character text uses `t = 0`.
- `gradient` interpolates in RGB space through `Color::lerp`, so palette
  indices interpolate in RGB too.
- `rainbow` maps `t` through `hsv_to_rgb(t × 360, 1.0, 1.0)` — fully
  saturated, full value, one hue per character.

The result prints like any line: it honors
[`ColorChoice`](/reference/color-control/) and degrades with
`render_with(level)`.

## hsv_to_rgb

`pub fn hsv_to_rgb(h: f32, s: f32, v: f32) -> (u8, u8, u8)` — the standard
HSV → RGB conversion. `h` is in degrees (values outside `0..360` wrap via
`rem_euclid`); `s` and `v` are in `0.0..=1.0`. Returns 8-bit components.

## Next steps

<!-- src/content/docs/reference/line.mdx -->
# Line

`Line` is an ordered sequence of [`Span`](/reference/span/)s that renders as a
single row. It derives `Debug`, `Clone`, `Default`, `PartialEq`, `Eq`, `Hash`.
Source: `src/line.rs`.

## Construction

| Member | Signature | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `new` | `pub const fn new() -> Self` | Empty line |
| `from_spans` | `pub fn from_spans(spans: impl IntoIterator<Item = Span>) -> Self` | From any span iterator |

## Pushing and editing spans

| Method | Signature | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `push` | `pub fn push(self, span: impl Into<Span>) -> Self` | Appends; builder style |
| `push_mut` | `pub fn push_mut(&mut self, span: impl Into<Span>)` | Appends in place |
| `extend` | `pub fn extend(self, spans: impl IntoIterator<Item = Span>) -> Self` | Appends several |
| `spans` | `pub fn spans(&self) -> &[Span]` | The pushed spans |
| `visible_width` | `pub fn visible_width(&self) -> usize` | Total CJK-aware width |

### The last-span rule

The style methods below apply to the **last pushed span**. If the line is
empty when one is called, an empty span is created first, so the call never
panics — it restyles an invisible segment.

| Group | Methods |
| --- | --- |
| Direct setters | `fg(Color)`, `bg(Color)`, `fg_rgb(u8, u8, u8)`, `bg_rgb(u8, u8, u8)`, `attr(Attribute)`, `effects(Effects)` |
| Foreground | `black`, `red`, `green`, `yellow`, `blue`, `magenta`, `cyan`, `white`, `bright_black`, `bright_red`, `bright_green`, `bright_yellow`, `bright_blue`, `bright_magenta`, `bright_cyan`, `bright_white` |
| Background | `on_black`, `on_red`, `on_green`, `on_yellow`, `on_blue`, `on_magenta`, `on_cyan`, `on_white`, `on_bright_black`, `on_bright_red`, `on_bright_green`, `on_bright_yellow`, `on_bright_blue`, `on_bright_magenta`, `on_bright_cyan`, `on_bright_white` |
| Attributes | `bold`, `dim`, `italic`, `underline`, `blink`, `reverse`, `hidden`, `strikethrough` |

## Whole-line operations

| Method | Signature | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `with_style` | `pub fn with_style(self, style: Style) -> Self` | Merges into **every** span; the merged style's colors win, attributes union |
| `map_span` | `pub fn map_span(self, f: impl FnMut(Span) -> Span) -> Self` | Rewrites each span |
| `when` | `pub fn when(self, condition: bool, f: impl FnOnce(Self) -> Self) -> Self` | Conditional builder |

## Rendering and printing

| Method | Signature | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `render` | `pub fn render(&self) -> String` | Deterministic |
| `render_with` | `pub fn render_with(&self, level: ColorLevel) -> String` | Degrades every span to `level` |
| `write_to` | `pub fn write_to(&self, writer: &mut impl io::Write) -> io::Result<()>` | Honors `ColorChoice`; fallible |
| `print` / `println` | stdout, without / with newline | Panics on failure |
| `eprint` / `eprintln` | stderr, without / with newline | Panics on failure |
| `try_print` / `try_println` | stdout, fallible | `io::Result<()>` |
| `try_eprint` / `try_eprintln` | stderr, fallible | `io::Result<()>` |

When printing with colors disabled, the plain concatenation of the spans'
text is written — no escapes at all. `Display` renders like `render`; a
format width pads by the line's total visible width, honoring the spec's fill
and alignment.

## Derives and trait impls

| Impl | Behavior |
| --- | --- |
| `Default` | Empty line |
| `From<&str>`, `From<String>` | One plain span |
| `From<Span>` | One-span line |
| `From<Vec<Span>>` | Direct |
| `FromIterator<Span>` | `collect()` support |
| `IntoIterator` | `Item = Span`, consumes the line |

## Next steps

<!-- src/content/docs/reference/macros.mdx -->
# Macros

Three declarative macros build styled values in one expression. They are
exported at the crate root (`#[macro_export]`). Source: `src/macros.rs`.

## paint!

`paint!(method+, format-args…) -> Span` — builds a
[`Span`](/reference/span/) from `format!` arguments and a list of style
method names:

```rust
use pretty_console::paint;

let msg = paint!(green bold, "{} tests passed", 12);
msg.println();
```

## style!

`style!(method+) -> Style` — builds a [`Style`](/reference/style/) the same
way:

```rust
use pretty_console::style;

let danger = style!(bold red on_white);
danger.paint("boom").println();
```

## line!

`line!(span, …) -> Line` — builds a [`Line`](/reference/line/) by pushing
each expression (spans or plain strings):

```rust
use pretty_console::line;

let row = line!("cache ", "warm", " · 42 entries");
row.println();
```

## Constraints

- The method list accepts any no-argument `Span`/`Style` builder method name:
  colors (`red`, `bright_blue`), backgrounds (`on_white`), attributes
  (`bold`, `underline`).
- Methods that take arguments — `fg_rgb`, `fg_hex`, `fg`, `bg`, `attr`,
  `effects` — cannot appear in the list; use the regular builder chain for
  those.
- The methods are applied left to right; because attributes are idempotent
  and colors overwrite, later names win.

## Next steps

import { LinkCard } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

<LinkCard title="Span" description="The builder methods the macros accept." href="/reference/span/" />

<!-- src/content/docs/reference/panel.mdx -->
# Panel

`Panel` renders a rounded box (`╭ ─ ╮ │ ╰ ─ ╯`) containing styled
[`Line`](/reference/line/)s with an optional title inlaid into the top
border. It derives `Debug`, `Clone`, `PartialEq`, `Eq`, `Hash`, and `Default`
equals `Panel::new()`. Source: `src/panel.rs`.

## Builder methods and defaults

| Method | Signature | Default | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `new` | `pub const fn new() -> Self` | — | Padding 1, plain border, no title, no fixed width |
| `title` | `pub fn title(self, title: impl Into<String>) -> Self` | none | Inlaid as `─ Title` (title, one space, then dashes) into the top border; the title keeps its own style |
| `line` | `pub fn line(self, line: impl Into<Line>) -> Self` | empty | Accepts a `Line`, a `Span`, or a plain string |
| `lines` | `pub fn lines(self, lines: impl IntoIterator<Item = impl Into<Line>>) -> Self` | empty | Appends several at once |
| `width` | `pub fn width(self, width: usize) -> Self` | none (auto) | Inner content width; see below |
| `padding` | `pub fn padding(self, padding: usize) -> Self` | `1` | Horizontal padding on each side of the content |
| `border` | `pub fn border(self, style: Style) -> Self` | plain | Styles the border characters and the title divider dashes |

Content spans keep their own styles; only border and divider characters take
the border style.

## Width computation

`content_width(&self) -> usize` returns the width between the vertical bars:

- with an explicit width: `(width + 2 × padding)`, raised to fit the title;
- without: `max(widest line) + 2 × padding`, raised to fit the title.

The title minimum is `visible_width(title) + 2 × padding + 1`.

With a fixed width, lines wider than the body are truncated with an ellipsis
(`…`); without one, the box grows to the widest line.

## Rendering

| Method | Signature | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `render` | `pub fn render(&self) -> String` | Deterministic |
| `render_plain` | `pub fn render_plain(&self) -> String` | All escapes stripped, for logs and tests |
| `write_to` | `pub fn write_to(&self, writer: &mut impl io::Write) -> io::Result<()>` | Honors `ColorChoice`; fallible |
| `print` | stdout | Panics on failure |
| `println` | stdout + newline | Panics on failure |

`Display` renders like `render`. Content lines are padded to the body width
with `pad` using visible width, so CJK content keeps the border aligned.

## Next steps

import { LinkCard } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

<!-- src/content/docs/reference/span.mdx -->
# Span

`Span` is a styled string: text, a [`Style`](/reference/style/), and an
optional OSC 8 hyperlink. It derives `Debug`, `Clone`, `Default`,
`PartialEq`, `Eq`, `Hash`, and implements `Display` with visible-width
padding. The v1 name `Console` survives as a type alias. Source:
`src/span.rs`.

## Constructors

| Method | Signature | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `new` | `pub fn new(text: impl Into<String>) -> Self` | Plain style, no link |
| `new_with_style` | `pub fn new_with_style(text: impl Into<String>, style: Style) -> Self` | Pre-built style |
| `with_style` | `pub fn with_style(text: impl Into<String>, style: Style) -> Self` | Alias of `new_with_style` |
| `with_text` | `pub fn with_text(&self, text: impl Into<String>) -> Self` | Keeps style and link, replaces text |
| `info` | `pub fn info(text: impl Into<String>) -> Self` | `[INFO]` prefix, cyan |
| `warn` | `pub fn warn(text: impl Into<String>) -> Self` | `[WARN]` prefix, yellow |
| `error` | `pub fn error(text: impl Into<String>) -> Self` | `[ERROR]` prefix, bold red |
| `success` | `pub fn success(text: impl Into<String>) -> Self` | `[OK]` prefix, bold green |
| `debug` | `pub fn debug(text: impl Into<String>) -> Self` | `[DEBUG]` prefix, dim |
| `banner` | `pub fn banner(title: impl Into<String>, width: usize) -> Self` | Full-width centered banner, cyan bold |

## Text and style accessors

| Method | Signature | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `text` | `pub fn text(&self) -> &str` | The unstyled text |
| `set_text` | `pub fn set_text(&mut self, text: impl Into<String>)` | In-place replacement |
| `style` | `pub const fn style(&self) -> &Style` | The held style |
| `set_style` | `pub fn set_style(&mut self, style: Style)` | In-place replacement |
| `styled_with` | `pub fn styled_with(self, style: Style) -> Self` | Builder form of `set_style` |

## Style builder methods

All builder methods consume `self` and return `Self`. Colors set the
foreground (`fg*`) or background (`bg*`, `on_*`) of the held style; attribute
methods insert into the style's [`Effects`](/reference/style/) bitset.

| Group | Methods |
| --- | --- |
| Direct setters | `fg(Color)`, `bg(Color)`, `fg_rgb(u8, u8, u8)`, `bg_rgb(u8, u8, u8)`, `fg_hex(u32)`, `bg_hex(u32)`, `attr(Attribute)`, `effects(Effects)` |
| Foreground | `black`, `red`, `green`, `yellow`, `blue`, `magenta`, `cyan`, `white`, `bright_black`, `bright_red`, `bright_green`, `bright_yellow`, `bright_blue`, `bright_magenta`, `bright_cyan`, `bright_white` |
| Background | `on_black`, `on_red`, `on_green`, `on_yellow`, `on_blue`, `on_magenta`, `on_cyan`, `on_white`, `on_bright_black`, `on_bright_red`, `on_bright_green`, `on_bright_yellow`, `on_bright_blue`, `on_bright_magenta`, `on_bright_cyan`, `on_bright_white` |
| Attributes | `bold`, `dim`, `italic`, `underline`, `blink`, `reverse`, `hidden`, `strikethrough` |
| Conditional | `when(bool, impl FnOnce(Self) -> Self)` |

## Level helpers

The constructors `info`, `warn`, `error`, `success` and `debug` prefix the
text with a tag and apply a fixed style:

| Constructor | Tag | Style |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `info` | `[INFO]` | cyan |
| `warn` | `[WARN]` | yellow |
| `error` | `[ERROR]` | bold red |
| `success` | `[OK]` | bold green |
| `debug` | `[DEBUG]` | dim |

## Banner

`banner(title, width)` builds a horizontal rule with the centered title,
styled cyan and bold. The rule character is `─`; the title width is measured
with `chars().count()`. When `width` is too small to leave at least two
dashes on each side (fewer than 4 dashes in total), the plain title styled
cyan and bold is returned instead.

## Hyperlinks

| Method | Signature | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `link` | `pub fn link(self, url: impl Into<Box<str>>) -> Self` | Attaches an OSC 8 URL |
| `unlink` | `pub fn unlink(self) -> Self` | Removes any URL |
| `url` | `pub fn url(&self) -> Option<&str>` | The current URL |

A link renders as `ESC ]8;;URL ESC \` before the styled text and
`ESC ]8;; ESC \` after it. Links are suppressed under the `no-color` feature
and when printing with colors disabled.

## Rendering

| Method | Signature | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `render` | `pub fn render(&self) -> String` | Deterministic; never consults the environment |
| `render_with` | `pub fn render_with(&self, level: ColorLevel) -> String` | Degrades colors to `level` first |
| `write_to` | `pub fn write_to(&self, writer: &mut impl io::Write) -> io::Result<()>` | Honors `ColorChoice`; fallible |

`Display` (and therefore `to_string`) renders like `render`. When a format
width is present, padding is computed from the visible (CJK-aware) text
width, honoring the spec's fill and alignment.

## Printing

All methods below write to stdout or stderr, honoring the global
[`ColorChoice`](/reference/color-control/).

| Method | Stream | Newline | Failure |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `print` | stdout | no | panics |
| `println` | stdout | yes | panics |
| `eprint` | stderr | no | panics |
| `eprintln` | stderr | yes | panics |
| `try_print` | stdout | no | `io::Result<()>` |
| `try_println` | stdout | yes | `io::Result<()>` |
| `try_eprint` | stderr | no | `io::Result<()>` |
| `try_eprintln` | stderr | yes | `io::Result<()>` |

## The Styled extension trait

`Styled` is implemented for every `T: AsRef<str> + ?Sized` and paints
string-like values in place. `styled()` wraps the value in a plain
`Span`; every other method forwards to the corresponding `Span` builder and
returns a `Span`:

```rust
use pretty_console::Styled;

let span = "hello".red().bold();
```

The trait carries `styled`, the sixteen foreground colors, the sixteen
`on_*` backgrounds, and the eight attribute methods — the same names as the
`Span` builder tables above.

## Derives and trait impls

| Impl | Behavior |
| --- | --- |
| `Default` | Empty text, plain style, no link |
| `From<&str>`, `From<String>` | Same as `Span::new` |
| `Display` | Render with visible-width padding |

`Console` is `pub type Console = Span;`, kept for v1 compatibility.

<!-- src/content/docs/reference/style.mdx -->
# Style, Attribute and Effects

`Style` bundles a foreground color, a background color and a set of text
attributes. It is `Copy`, `const`-constructible, and never allocates.
`Attribute` is the enum of the eight SGR attributes; `Effects` is the `u16`
bitset that stores them. Sources: `src/style.rs`, `src/attr.rs`.

## Style

Derives `Debug`, `Clone`, `Copy`, `Default`, `PartialEq`, `Eq`, `Hash`.

| Member | Signature | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `new` | `pub const fn new() -> Self` | No colors, no attributes |
| `fg` | `pub const fn fg(self, color: Color) -> Self` | Sets foreground |
| `bg` | `pub const fn bg(self, color: Color) -> Self` | Sets background |
| `attr` | `pub const fn attr(self, attribute: Attribute) -> Self` | Inserts one attribute |
| `effects` | `pub const fn effects(self, effects: Effects) -> Self` | Unions a set |
| `foreground` | `pub const fn foreground(&self) -> Option<Color>` | Get foreground |
| `background` | `pub const fn background(&self) -> Option<Color>` | Get background |
| `attributes` | `pub const fn attributes(&self) -> Effects` | Get the bitset |
| `is_plain` | `pub const fn is_plain(&self) -> bool` | No colors and no attributes |
| `merge` | `pub const fn merge(self, other: Self) -> Self` | Colors of `other` win; attributes union |
| `degraded` | `pub fn degraded(&self, level: ColorLevel) -> Self` | Reduces both colors to `level` |
| `paint` | `pub fn paint(self, text: impl Into<String>) -> Span` | Produces a `Span` |
| `to_ansi_start` | `pub fn to_ansi_start(&self) -> String` | The SGR start sequence; empty when plain |
| `when` | `pub fn when(self, condition: bool, f: impl FnOnce(Self) -> Self) -> Self` | Conditional builder |

`Style` also carries the same builder method names as
[`Span`](/reference/span/): sixteen foreground colors, sixteen `on_*`
backgrounds, eight attribute methods — all `const fn`.

### Merge semantics

`self.merge(other)`:

- foreground: `other`'s if set, otherwise `self`'s;
- background: `other`'s if set, otherwise `self`'s;
- attributes: the union of both sets — no duplicates can appear.

### Trait impls

| Impl | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `From<Color>` | `Style::new().fg(color)` |
| `From<Effects>` | `Style::new().effects(effects)` |
| `From<Attribute>` | `Style::new().attr(attribute)` |

## Attribute

Derives `Debug`, `Clone`, `Copy`, `PartialEq`, `Eq`, `Hash`.

| Variant | SGR code | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Bold` | `1` | Bold or increased intensity |
| `Dim` | `2` | Decreased intensity |
| `Italic` | `3` | Italic |
| `Underline` | `4` | Underlined |
| `Blink` | `5` | Slow blink |
| `Reverse` | `7` | Reverse video |
| `Hidden` | `8` | Concealed |
| `Strikethrough` | `9` | Strikethrough |

| Member | Signature | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `ALL` | `pub const ALL: [Attribute; 8]` | Canonical emission order |
| `code` | `pub const fn code(self) -> &'static str` | The SGR parameter above |
| `bit` | `pub const fn bit(self) -> u16` | Its bit inside `Effects` |
| `bit_index` | `pub const fn bit_index(self) -> u16` | Position 0–7 |

## Effects

A compact `Copy` bitset over the eight attributes; derives `Debug`, `Clone`,
`Copy`, `Default`, `PartialEq`, `Eq`, `Hash`. Adding an attribute is a single
`or`, duplicates are impossible, and every operation is `const`.

| Member | Signature | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `EMPTY` | `pub const EMPTY: Self` | No attributes |
| `BOLD` … `STRIKETHROUGH` | one `pub const` per attribute | Single-bit sets |
| `ALL` | `pub const ALL: Self` | `0x00FF` |
| `from_bits` | `pub const fn from_bits(bits: u16) -> Self` | Unknown bits masked off |
| `bits` | `pub const fn bits(self) -> u16` | Raw bits |
| `is_empty` | `pub const fn is_empty(self) -> bool` | No attribute set |
| `contains` | `pub const fn contains(self, other: Self) -> bool` | Superset test |
| `has` | `pub const fn has(self, attribute: Attribute) -> bool` | Single-attribute test |
| `insert` | `pub const fn insert(self, attribute: Attribute) -> Self` | Adds one attribute |
| `remove` | `pub const fn remove(self, attribute: Attribute) -> Self` | Removes one attribute |
| `union` | `pub const fn union(self, other: Self) -> Self` | Bitwise or |
| `without` | `pub const fn without(self, other: Self) -> Self` | Difference |
| `attributes` | `pub fn attributes(self) -> EffectIter` | Iterator in canonical order |

Operators: `BitOr`/`BitOrAssign` forward to `union`; `Sub` forwards to
`without`. `Display` prints the set's SGR parameters joined with `;` — an
empty set prints nothing.

## EffectIter

`EffectIter` is the iterator produced by `Effects::attributes`. It yields
`Attribute` items in canonical emission order (bold → strikethrough) and
implements `ExactSizeIterator`. It is `Copy` — a cursor over the bitset,
cheaper to copy than to borrow.

<!-- src/content/docs/reference/text-tools.mdx -->
# Text tools

The text utilities treat ANSI escape sequences as zero-width, skip zero-width
characters and count wide characters as two columns, so measurements match
what a terminal renders. They are dependency-free and use a practical
approximation of the `unicode-width` reference tables. Source: `src/text.rs`.

## strip_ansi

`pub fn strip_ansi(input: &str) -> String` — removes escape sequences and
returns the plain text.

Recognized sequences:

| Form | Grammar |
| --- | --- |
| CSI | `ESC [` + any number of parameter/intermediate bytes (`0x20..=0x3F`) + exactly one final byte |
| OSC | `ESC ]` + payload until `BEL` (`0x07`) or `ESC \` (ST) |
| Other | `ESC` plus exactly one following character |

Truncated sequences at the end of the input are dropped.

## char_width

`pub fn char_width(c: char) -> usize` — the number of terminal columns one
character occupies.

| Range | Width |
| --- | --- |
| Control characters `0x00..=0x1F`, `0x7F` | 0 |
| Combining diacritics and marks (e.g. `0x0300..=0x036F`, `0x0591..=0x05BD`, `0x20D0..=0x20F0`) | 0 |
| Zero-width space, ZWNJ, ZWJ, directional marks (`0x200B..=0x200F`, `0x2060..=0x2064`, `0xFEFF`) | 0 |
| Variation selectors (`0xFE00..=0xFE0F`, `0xE0100..=0xE01EF`) | 0 |
| Hangul Jamo (`0x1100..=0x115F`) | 2 |
| CJK radicals, punctuation, kana, ideographs (`0x2E80..=0x33FF`, `0x3400..=0x4DBF`, `0x4E00..=0x9FFF`) | 2 |
| Yi, Hangul jamo and syllables (`0xA000..=0xA4CF`, `0xA960..=0xA97F`, `0xAC00..=0xD7A3`) | 2 |
| CJK compatibility forms (`0xF900..=0xFAFF`, `0xFE10..=0xFE19`, `0xFE30..=0xFE6F`) | 2 |
| Fullwidth forms (`0xFF00..=0xFF60`, `0xFFE0..=0xFFE6`) | 2 |
| Emoji blocks (`0x1F300..=0x1F64F`, `0x1F900..=0x1F9FF`, `0x1FA70..=0x1FAFF`) | 2 |
| CJK extensions B and C (`0x20000..=0x2FFFD`, `0x30000..=0x3FFFD`) | 2 |
| Everything else | 1 |

This is a documented approximation chosen to keep the crate dependency-free;
it does not reach full parity with the `unicode-width` crate.

## visible_width

`pub fn visible_width(input: &str) -> usize` — the number of terminal columns
`input` occupies.

- If the input contains `ESC`, it is stripped first, then measured.
- Pure-ASCII inputs count the printable bytes `0x20..=0x7E` (a fast path).
- Otherwise the widths of the characters are summed.

## truncate

`pub fn truncate(input: &str, max_width: usize, tail: &str) -> String` — cuts
to at most `max_width` visible columns, appending `tail` when truncation
happens.

| Behavior | Detail |
| --- | --- |
| Fits | Returned unchanged (a fresh `String`) |
| Budget | Characters keep fitting while `width + char_width ≤ max_width − visible_width(tail)` |
| Escapes | Preserved and zero-width; a reset (`ESC [0m`) is appended after the tail when any escape was emitted |
| Undersized budget | When `max_width` is smaller than the tail, the tail overruns the requested width |

## pad and Align

`pub fn pad(input: &str, width: usize, align: Align, fill: char) -> String` —
pads to exactly `width` visible columns.

| Case | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Input wider than `width` | Returned unchanged — `pad` never truncates |
| `Align::Left` (default) | Fill appended on the right |
| `Align::Center` | Split, the odd column on the right |
| `Align::Right` | Fill prepended on the left |

`Align` derives `Debug`, `Clone`, `Copy`, `Default`, `PartialEq`, `Eq`,
`Hash`; `Default` is `Left`.

## Next steps

<!-- src/content/docs/tutorials/getting-started.mdx -->
# Getting started

import { LinkCard, Tabs, TabItem, Steps, Aside } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

This tutorial takes you from an empty directory to a running program that
prints styled spans and a multi-segment line. You will see visible results at
every step. The whole tutorial uses one path with no alternatives.

## Prerequisites

- The Rust toolchain, version 1.85 or newer (`rustc --version` to confirm).
- A terminal.

## What you will build

A tiny program that prints:

1. one styled span — bold red text,
2. one styled string literal — cyan, written in place,
3. one multi-segment line — dim label, bold command, green duration.

## Build and run

<Steps>

1. **Create a project.** In your terminal, create a new Rust project and move
   into it:

   ```sh
   cargo new pretty-demo
   cd pretty-demo
   ```

2. **Add the crate.**

   <Tabs>
     <TabItem label="cargo add">

   ```sh
   cargo add pretty-console
   ```

     </TabItem>
     <TabItem label="Cargo.toml">

   Add the dependency to the `[dependencies]` section of `Cargo.toml`:

   ```toml
   [dependencies]
   pretty-console = "2.0.0"
   ```

     </TabItem>
   </Tabs>

   You should now see `Adding pretty-console v2.0.0` (or a newer patch) in the
   output.

3. **Style a single span.** Open `src/main.rs` and replace its contents with:

   ```rust
   use pretty_console::{Span, Styled};

   fn main() {
       Span::new("Hello, world!").red().bold().println();
   }
   ```

   Every builder call — `.red()`, `.bold()` — returns the span again, so calls
   chain left to right. `.println()` writes the result to stdout. Run it:

   ```sh
   cargo run
   ```

   You should now see **Hello, world!** printed in bold red.

   <Aside type="note">
     If your terminal does not support colors (for example in some CI logs),
     the same text appears without escapes — printing detects that case for
     you.
   </Aside>

4. **Style a literal in place.** The `Styled` trait paints string literals
   directly, without constructing a `Span` by hand. Add a second line to
   `main`:

   ```rust
   use pretty_console::{Span, Styled};

   fn main() {
       Span::new("Hello, world!").red().bold().println();
       println!("{}", "Ready to go".cyan());
   }
   ```

   Run it again:

   ```sh
   cargo run
   ```

   You should now see both lines: the bold red greeting, then **Ready to go**
   in cyan.

5. **Compose a multi-segment line.** Real CLIs print rows where each segment
   carries its own style. `Line` joins spans into one row, and its styling
   methods apply to the segment you pushed last:

   ```rust
   use pretty_console::{Line, Span, Styled};

   fn main() {
       Span::new("Hello, world!").red().bold().println();
       println!("{}", "Ready to go".cyan());

       Line::new()
           .push("  build ").dim()
           .push("cargo build --release").bold()
           .push(" finished in ").push("4.2s").green()
           .println();
   }
   ```

   The third line reads left to right: a dim label, a bold command, a plain
   connector, and a green duration — because `.green()` styles the last pushed
   segment, `"4.2s"`. Run the final version:

   ```sh
   cargo run
   ```

   You should now see three rows:

   - **Hello, world!** — bold red
   - **Ready to go** — cyan
   - `build cargo build --release finished in 4.2s` — preceded by two spaces,
     with the label dimmed, the command bold, and `4.2s` green

</Steps>

## Where to go next

You have the core workflow. The pages below take the next step in each
direction.

<LinkCard title="Reuse and merge styles" description="Define a style once and apply it to many strings." href="/guides/reusable-styles/" />
